claims.text: Local chemical short-range order produces spatial fluctuations in shear-fault energy in multi-component concentrated alloys.
Spatial fluctuations in shear-fault energy lead to heterogeneous lattice strain.
Heterogeneous lattice strain and the associated energy landscape pin dislocations.
Short-range order and spatial fault-energy fluctuations cause dislocations in complex concentrated alloys to adopt wavy configurations.
Fault-energy fluctuations increase the stress required for dislocation motion and are a primary origin of strength in complex concentrated alloys.
The heterogeneous energy landscape activates additional slip systems.
The proposed dislocation interactions enhance strain hardening.
A fully recrystallized FCC NiCoCr alloy exhibits local chemical short-range order and heterogeneous lattice strain.
Alloys with one or two principal elements have a more homogeneous lattice-energy landscape and less pronounced dislocation pinning than multi-component concentrated alloys.
At matched grain size, phase constitution, and test conditions, a multi-component concentrated alloy will have higher yield strength than a simpler alloy.
At matched grain size, phase constitution, and test conditions, a multi-component concentrated alloy will have a higher strain-hardening rate than a simpler alloy.
Multi-component concentrated alloys will show more distinct wavy dislocation configurations than the simpler baseline alloy.
Testing at 77 K limits thermally activated processes while retaining dislocation-mediated plasticity as the dominant deformation mode.
The proposed mechanism should govern only before twinning or transformation-induced plasticity becomes significant.
The controlled comparison uses similar grain size and phase constitution and identical processing and mechanical-test conditions.
